title: Netiquette, E-Commerce & Digital Divide
short: Good behaviour online, safe buying and banking, and who gets left offline.
lede: Unit III is about responsible behaviour: how to act, how to transact, and who the internet still leaves out.
lens: List netiquette rules; explain e-commerce privacy, fraud and secure transmission; define the digital divide and freedom of information.
**Unit III is only 10 marks of short answers** — learn each idea as a crisp definition plus two examples.
concepts: **1. Netiquette.** **Netiquette** (network + etiquette) is the code of good manners for the internet: write polite messages, respect other people’s time and privacy, do not type in ALL CAPS (it reads as shouting), do not forward rumours or spam, and give credit instead of copying. Schools test it as a short list of do’s and don’ts.

**2. E-commerce.** **E-commerce** means buying, selling, banking and paying over the internet — e-shopping, e-banking, e-reservation, online bill payment. It is fast and available round the clock, but every transaction moves money and personal data, so privacy and fraud are the two big risks.

**3. Privacy and fraud.** **Privacy** means your personal data (name, address, card number, OTP) must stay with the parties you trust — never share passwords or OTPs, and check what an app collects before installing it. **Fraud** is cheating online: fake shops that take payment and never deliver, phishing messages that steal passwords, and lottery/prize scams. The defence is simple — shop on known sites, look for `https://`, and never pay in advance to strangers.

**4. Secure data transmission.** Data is protected in transit by **encryption** (scrambling it so only the receiver can read it), by **`https://`** (HTTP over a secure channel — the padlock in the browser), by **OTPs** (one-time passwords that prove it is really you), and by **firewalls and updated software** on both ends. `http://` without the *s* sends everything as readable text.

**5. Freedom of information.** **Freedom of information** is the principle that citizens have the right to access information — governments publish records, results and services online (e-governance) so that people can see, question and use them. It sits opposite censorship: an open internet lets ideas and facts flow freely.

**6. Digital divide.** The **digital divide** is the gap between people who have access to computers, smartphones and the internet — and those who do not, because of poverty, remote villages, age, language or disability. Consequences: missed schooling (online classes), missed services (banking, certificates) and missed opportunities. It is bridged by cheap devices, mobile networks in villages, public Wi-Fi and services in regional languages.
tricks: - **Netiquette = manners with a modem.** Polite words, no CAPS, no spam, give credit.
- **Shop SAFE: Secure site, Avoid advance payment, Fraud-check the seller, Exit if it smells wrong.**
- **Divide = the offline gap.** Access + skills + language decide who is in.
mistakes: - Calling any online cheating “hacking” — shopping fraud, phishing and fake shops each have their own name.
- Saying `http` is safe — only **`https`** encrypts the data in transit.
- Defining the digital divide as only “no internet” — devices, skills, language and cost count too.
- Sharing an OTP “even with the bank” — no genuine caller ever asks for it.

qa.q: What is netiquette? List any four netiquette rules.
qa.a: **Netiquette** (network + etiquette) is the code of polite, responsible behaviour on the internet. Four rules: (1) write courteous messages and respect others’ privacy; (2) do not type in ALL CAPS — it reads as shouting; (3) do not forward rumours, chain messages or spam; (4) give credit for others’ work instead of copying it.

qa.q: What is e-commerce? Give two examples from the syllabus.
qa.a: **E-commerce** means carrying out trade — buying, selling, paying and banking — over the internet. Two syllabus examples: **e-shopping** (ordering goods on a website) and **e-banking** (transferring money or paying bills through a bank’s site or app). e-reservation and online bill payment are two more.

qa.q: Why is privacy the biggest concern in e-commerce? State two precautions a buyer should take.
qa.a: Every e-commerce transaction moves **money plus personal data** (name, address, card number, OTP), which thieves can misuse. Two precautions: (1) shop only on known, reputed sites showing **`https://`** and the padlock; (2) **never share passwords or OTPs** with anyone, and check what data an app collects before installing it.

qa.q: What is the digital divide?
qa.a: The **digital divide** is the gap between people who have access to computers, smartphones and the internet — and those who do not. It is caused by poverty, remote villages with no network, lack of digital skills, age, disability and language barriers, and it locks the excluded out of online schooling, banking and services.

qa.q: Explain online fraud in e-commerce with two examples. How can a buyer avoid each?
qa.a: **Online fraud** is cheating a buyer or seller over the internet. Example 1: **fake shops** that take payment and never deliver — avoid by buying only from known sites and checking reviews. Example 2: **phishing** messages that pose as a bank and steal passwords — avoid by never clicking such links and never sharing OTPs.

qa.q: How is data kept secure during transmission? Explain any three methods.
qa.a: Three methods: (1) **Encryption** — scrambling the data so only the intended receiver can read it. (2) **`https://`** — HTTP over a secure channel (the browser padlock); plain `http` sends everything as readable text. (3) **OTPs** — one-time passwords sent to the buyer’s phone that prove the transaction is really theirs.

qa.q: What is freedom of information? How does e-governance support it?
qa.a: **Freedom of information** is the principle that citizens have the right to access information held by public authorities. **E-governance** supports it by putting records, results, forms and services online — certificates, exam results, land records — so people can see, question and use them without middlemen or secrecy.

qa.q: State three consequences of the digital divide and three ways to bridge it.
qa.a: Consequences: students miss **online classes**, citizens miss **digital banking and certificates**, and job-seekers miss **online opportunities**. Bridging it: (1) cheap smartphones and low-cost data; (2) mobile networks and public Wi-Fi in villages; (3) services and training in **regional languages** so language is no barrier.

qa.q: A friend forwards every “forward to 10 people” message, types angry replies in CAPS, and posts a classmate’s photo without asking. Which three netiquette rules is being broken, and what should be done instead?
a: Chain forwards break the **no spam/rumours** rule — verify before forwarding, or delete.
ALL-CAPS replies break the **no shouting** rule — use normal case and polite words.
Posting the photo breaks **respect for privacy** — always take permission before sharing someone’s picture or number.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

Meera finds a phone 40% cheaper on an unknown site. The site uses `http://`, asks for full payment by bank transfer, and a “seller” on chat asks for her OTP to “confirm the order”.

(a) Name three fraud/danger signals.
(b) What should Meera do?
a: (a) An unknown site with an **unbelievable discount**; **`http://` with no padlock**, so data travels unencrypted; and **advance bank transfer plus an OTP demand** — no genuine seller ever asks for an OTP.
(b) Close the site, buy only from a reputed `https://` shop, never pay strangers in advance, and never share the OTP with anyone.

qa.q:
Read and answer:

A village gets a mobile tower but students still cannot attend online classes: families share one old phone, the signal is weak indoors, and the learning app is English-only.

(a) Which problem is this an example of?
(b) Identify three barriers shown here.
(c) Suggest one fix for each.
a: (a) This is the **digital divide** — access on paper, exclusion in practice.
(b) Shared/old **devices**, weak **connectivity**, and a **language** barrier.
(c) Device: a shared tablet corner at school; connectivity: classes or downloads from a spot with signal; language: apps and help in the regional language.

qa.q: Responsible use of the internet needs good manners, safe transactions and access for all. Discuss netiquette, e-commerce safety and the digital divide.
a: **Netiquette** — polite messages, no CAPS shouting, no spam or rumours, respect privacy, give credit.

**E-commerce safety** — shop on reputed `https://` sites, guard privacy (no OTP/password sharing), recognise **fraud** (fake shops, phishing, prize scams), and rely on **secure transmission** (encryption, OTPs).

**Digital divide** — the gap between the connected and the unconnected, caused by cost, coverage, skills and language; bridged by cheap devices, village networks, public Wi-Fi and regional-language services.
Together the three ideas make one point: use the net politely, transact on it safely, and carry everyone along.

mcq.q: Typing a message in ALL CAPS is bad netiquette because it — (a) saves time (b) reads as shouting (c) looks stylish (d) avoids spam
mcq.a: **(b) reads as shouting.** Netiquette asks for normal case and polite words.

mcq.q: Which of these is an e-commerce activity? (a) reading a blog (b) paying an electricity bill on a bank app (c) watching a video (d) typing a document
mcq.a: **(b) paying an electricity bill on a bank app.** E-commerce = trade, payment and banking online.

mcq.q: A safe shopping site must show — (a) `http://` (b) `https://` with a padlock (c) flashing ads (d) pop-up prizes
mcq.a: **(b) `https://` with a padlock.** The *s* means the data is encrypted in transit.

mcq.q: Someone calls “from the bank” and asks for your OTP. You should — (a) share it quickly (b) share half of it (c) refuse and cut the call (d) ask for a bigger limit
mcq.a: **(c) refuse and cut the call.** No genuine caller ever asks for an OTP.

mcq.q: Phishing is an example of — (a) netiquette (b) online fraud (c) e-governance (d) encryption
mcq.a: **(b) online fraud.** Fake messages steal passwords and money.

mcq.q: The digital divide is the gap between — (a) boys and girls (b) the connected and the unconnected (c) cities (d) phones and laptops
mcq.a: **(b) the connected and the unconnected.** Cost, coverage, skills and language cause it.

mcq.q: Publishing exam results and certificates online is an example of — (a) e-governance supporting freedom of information (b) phishing (c) netiquette (d) malware
mcq.a: **(a) e-governance supporting freedom of information.** Citizens can see and use public records directly.

mcq.q: Which step does NOT bridge the digital divide? (a) village mobile networks (b) regional-language apps (c) English-only services (d) low-cost data
mcq.a: **(c) English-only services.** Services in regional languages include more people, not fewer.

trend: Short 2–3 mark definitions: one netiquette list, one e-commerce safety question, one digital-divide question.
onepager: - Netiquette: polite, no CAPS, no spam, privacy, credit.
- E-commerce: shopping/banking online; risks = privacy + fraud.
- Fraud: fake shops, phishing, prize scams — verify, never prepay strangers, never share OTP.
- Freedom of information + e-governance: public records online.
- Digital divide: the offline gap; fix with devices, coverage, regional languages.

**2.** Add two examples or two precautions — that is where the marks sit.

title: Cybercrime, IPR & Open Source
short: Cybercrime, intellectual property rights, plagiarism, and free versus open source software.
lede: Definitions plus one table. IPR is where students lose marks through vagueness.
lens: Define IPR and its types, explain plagiarism and software piracy, distinguish FOSS from proprietary software.
**Be precise about the four IPR types.**
concepts: **1. Cybercrime.** A **cybercrime** is any illegal act in which a computer or network is used as a tool, a target, or a place to store evidence. Examples are hacking, spreading malware, online fraud, identity theft, publishing obscene material, and attacking a website so that it stops working.

**2. Intellectual property rights.** **IPR** is the legal right given to the creator of an original work, so that others cannot copy or profit from it without permission. The four main types are: **copyright**, which protects original literary, artistic, musical and software works; **patent**, which protects an invention or process for a fixed period; **trademark**, which protects a brand name, logo or slogan; and **trade secret**, which protects confidential business information such as a recipe or a formula.

**3. Violations.** **Software piracy** is copying, distributing or using software without a licence. **Plagiarism** is presenting someone else's words, ideas or code as your own, even with no money involved — which is what makes it an ethical offence as well as a legal one. Both are avoided by citing sources properly and using only licensed or freely licensed material.

**4. FOSS versus proprietary.** **Free and Open Source Software (FOSS)** can be used, studied, modified and redistributed by anyone because its **source code is available**; examples are **Linux**, **Firefox** and **LibreOffice**. **Free software** here means freedom, not necessarily zero price. **Proprietary software** keeps its source code secret and restricts copying and modification under a licence; examples are **Microsoft Windows** and **Adobe Photoshop**. **Freeware** is free to use but closed, and **shareware** is free to try for a limited period before payment.

Protects
Example
rows: Original literary, artistic, musical and software works
A novel, a song, a program

tricks: - **Copyright = works, patent = inventions, trademark = brands, trade secret = secrets.**
- **Piracy involves money or licences; plagiarism involves credit.**
- **FOSS = source code is open.** Free as in freedom, not free as in price.
- **Freeware is closed but free; shareware is a paid trial.**
mistakes: - Confusing **copyright and patent** — copyright covers creative works, patent covers inventions.
- Confusing **plagiarism with piracy** — plagiarism is taking credit, piracy is unlicensed copying.
- Saying FOSS is free **because it costs nothing** — it is free because the source is open.
- Listing **freeware as open source** — freeware is usually closed source.

qa.q: What is plagiarism and how can it be avoided?
qa.a: **Plagiarism** is presenting someone else's words, ideas, data or code as if they were your own, without giving credit. It is an ethical offence even when no money changes hands. It is avoided by always **citing the source**, using quotation marks around copied text, paraphrasing genuinely rather than swapping a few words, and keeping a record of every source consulted while working.

qa.q: What is software piracy?
qa.a: **Software piracy** is the unauthorised copying, distribution or use of software without a valid licence. It includes installing one licensed copy on many machines, downloading cracked versions, and selling counterfeit discs. It deprives developers of income and often exposes the user to malware, since pirated copies are frequently bundled with it.

qa.q: Distinguish between freeware and shareware.
qa.a: **Freeware** can be used free of charge indefinitely, but its source code is usually closed and it cannot be modified or sold — an example is Skype. **Shareware** is distributed free only as a trial, either for a limited period or with reduced features, and the user must pay to continue using it after the trial ends.

qa.q: What is plagiarism and how is it different from quoting?
qa.a: Plagiarism is using someone else's words, ideas, images or code and presenting them as your own, even if you change a few words or do not name the source. Quoting keeps the original wording inside quotation marks and names the author and the work, so the reader knows whose words they are; that is allowed and expected in school work.

qa.q: What is IPR? Name and explain its four main types.
qa.a: **IPR (Intellectual Property Rights)** are the legal rights granted to the creator of an original work, allowing them to control and benefit from its use and stopping others from copying it without permission. The four main types are **copyright**, which protects original literary, artistic, musical and software works; **patent**, which protects an invention or process for a fixed period; **trademark**, which protects a brand name, logo or slogan; and **trade secret**, which protects confidential business information such as a formula or a method.

qa.q: Differentiate between free and open source software and proprietary software, with examples.
qa.a: **FOSS** makes the **source code available**, so anyone may use, study, modify and redistribute the program; examples are Linux, Firefox and LibreOffice. Here 'free' refers to freedom rather than price. **Proprietary software** keeps its source code secret and grants only a licence to use it, forbidding copying, modification or redistribution; examples are Microsoft Windows and Adobe Photoshop. The practical difference is that with FOSS you can fix or extend the software yourself, while with proprietary software you depend entirely on the vendor.

qa.q: Riya is revising “Cybercrime, IPR & Open Source” (Cybercrime, intellectual property rights, plagiarism, and free versus open source software.). A classmate lost marks by doing this: Confusing copyright and patent — copyright covers creative works, patent covers inventions. Apply the correct method and rewrite the scoring answer.
a: Correct method: Copyright = works, patent = inventions, trademark = brands, trade secret = secrets.
Why the mistake costs marks: Confusing copyright and patent — copyright covers creative works, patent covers inventions.

qa.q: Amit is given this exam-style task from “Cybercrime, IPR & Open Source”: “What is IPR? Name and explain its four main types.” Treat it as an application question. Identify the idea, then write the working in points.
a: Idea: Cybercrime, intellectual property rights, plagiarism, and free versus open source software..

IPR (Intellectual Property Rights) are the legal rights granted to the creator of an original work, allowing them to control and benefit from its use and stopping others from copying it without permission. The four main types are copyright, which protects original literary, artistic, musical and software works; patent, which protects an invention or process for a fixed period; trademark, which protects a brand name, logo or slogan; and trade secret, which protects confidential business information such as a formula or a method.

qa.q: Explain the four main kinds of intellectual property.
a: Copyright protects original literary, musical, artistic and software works, and lasts for the life of the author plus sixty years in India.
A patent protects a new invention for twenty years, and lets the owner stop others from making or selling it.
A trademark protects a name, logo or symbol that identifies a business or product, such as a brand name or a jingle.
A design right protects the shape, pattern or look of a manufactured article, and trade secrets protect information kept confidential by a business.

mcq.q: Which IPR protects a brand logo? (a) copyright (b) patent (c) trademark (d) trade secret
Which IPR protects an invention? (a) copyright (b) patent (c) trademark (d) licence

mcq.q: Open source software is software that: (a) lets users study, change and share the source code  (b) is always free of cost  (c) cannot be copied  (d) runs only on mobile phones
